articles.title: Can RBI’s six forex measures help stabilise the rupee?
articles.text: Kolkata: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has taken a slew of steps since Saturday to help lift the rupee to what Governor Sanjay Malhotra described as its "correct" value. These measures have helped the rupee recover to 95.28 a dollar, about 150 paise over two days. An immediate fallout is the reduction in speculative bets on the currency and discouraging over-hedging by companies in anticipation of further rupee depreciation. An inevitable inflation in hedging costs, a natural outcome of the reserves to be set aside by banks against client exposures, has caused some noses to wrinkle in the importer community.Separately, total removal of the dollar needs of three state-run fuel retailers from the spot rupee market reduces the pressure on the currency.Here's an ET explainer on the measures taken by the central bank and their impact.Introduction of Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR)A first-time measure imposing a 20% cash reserve requirement on large forex derivatives contracts over $2 million. This means banks will have to set aside funds as a percentage of their total exposure, and that money will no longer be available for onlending until the exposure is fully cancelled.For instance, for a $10 million hedging contract for a client, a bank will have to keep around ₹19 crore everyday with the central bank until the expiry of the contract. This money is not available for lending.Hence, banks will have to pass on this cost to their clients. This would inflate the hedging cost for importers by at least 150 basis points (one basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point) and, therefore, they would be discouraged to hedge their exposure, experts said.Read more: Anand Rathi Share and Stock Brokers Q2 results: Profit jumps 50% YoY to Rs 42 crore, revenue rises 20%FERR Impact on the Forwards MarketsAnother fallout of the FERR curbs is an immediate cut in the rates on forward premium, as the aggregate demand for hedging itself would reduce. Since importers would keep open positions, it would ultimately soften forward premium rates, currency experts believe. Softening forward premiums will also help reduce pressure on the spot rupee in the local market.However, a section of the importers is worried their cost would climb significantly as the funds needed to hedge will eat into their working capital buffers, potentially requiring them to borrow to plug the gap.Read more: Strong buzz! Reliance Jio said to see over $20 billion bids as investors line up for India's biggest IPOExtension of FERR restrictions for contracts with overseas entitiesThe regulator Monday widened the ambit of FERR, extending the rule for non-deliverable contracts involving rupee to non-resident customers, only for the purpose of hedging. The move also eliminates the probability of dollar hoarding by companies and importers because of the steep FERR costs, limiting their dollar exposure to genuine and foreseeable business needs.Threshold for foreign exchange derivative transactions reducedThe limit has been reduced to $5 million equivalent from $100 million across all authorised dealers. This will curb speculative trading in the rupee. A corresponding reduction has been introduced in exchange-traded currency derivatives involving the rupee, across stock exchanges taken together.Restrictions on rebooking of cancelled foreign exchange derivative contractsBanks cannot allow users to rebook any previously cancelled foreign exchange derivative contract involving the rupee - whether deliverable or non-deliverable. Rollover of foreign exchange derivative contracts on maturity shall continue to be permitted.Special dollar window for State-run oil retailersThe RBI would use its own dollar stockpile to meet the daily dollar needs of Indian Oil Corp, Bharat Petroleum Corp and Hindustan Petroleum Corp. This reduces dollar demand in the spot market, easing the pressure on rupee.This would also mask the underlying pressure on balance of payments while dollars will be drained from the central bank's foreign exchange reservess. The Reserve Bank of India opened this window Monday, albeit for a temporary period.Stricter verificationRBI tells banks to obtain additional documentation for verification of underlying exposures. This will prevent users from entering into foreign exchange derivative contracts involving the rupee to hedge contracted exposures, using the same underlying exposure that has been hedged with any other bank. Banks have to keep the documents for a minimum two-year period.Overall views of forex market and treasury professionalsEconomists see these measures as tactical steps to support the rupee, not structural solutions ensuring its durable stability. They believe that defending the rupee amid the continued geopolitical headwinds would be a costly policy trade-off, requiring broader capital market reforms to encourage stable and long term foreign capital inflows.India still levies a security transactions tax, even when the long-term capital gains tax was reintroduced in 2018, and increased it to 12.5% last year. Experts suggest a broader response spanning lowering of taxes, exchange-rate flexibility and further monetary policy tightening to bolster the rupee.

articles.title: Martin Shkreli livestreamed himself violating lifetime pharma ban, FTC says
articles.text:
Martin Shkreli—the ex-pharmaceutical executive infamous for illegally hiking the price of a lifesaving anti-parasitic drug by more than 4,000 percent and getting a seven-year prison sentence for the fraudulent scheme he used to do it—has been under a lifetime ban from the pharmaceutical industry since 2022.

However, according to the Federal Trade Commission and the attorneys general of seven states, Shkreli has "flagrantly and repeatedly" violated that ban nearly the entire time—allegedly by trading stock in dozens of drug companies and discussing the industry during livestreams on social media.

On Tuesday, the FTC and the seven states asked a federal judge to hold Shkreli in contempt for the alleged violations. The states include New York, California, Illinois, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Virginia—the same states that joined the FTC in suing Shkreli in 2020 over the "elaborate anticompetitive scheme" involving the anti-parasitic drug, Daraprim. The scheme raised the price from $17.50 per pill to $750 per pill virtually overnight, while blocking generic competitors from entering the market.

articles.title: Anthropic reinvents source control as Claude floods the world with code
articles.text: Anthropic's Claude models have been emitting so much code that the company's coding infrastructure hasn't been able to keep up. It's a symptom of the AI coding imperative and all-you-can-eat inference. Microsoft's GitHub in April published a blog post attributing recent availability problems to the exponential growth in pull requests and commits. The code flood has been noted by academic researchers, among others. For Anthropic, writing code is no longer a productivity bottleneck. Instead, the problem is managing the code after it's written, via source control, the build system, and continuous integration. "In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day," the biz said in a blog post on Tuesday. "We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce." After several months of model prompting and five months of migration, the result is a homemade version control system called Scion, a monorepo scheme that sounds a bit like Subversion, Apache's centralized version control system. Anthropic is not the first organization to look beyond Git's distributed architecture toward centralized source control. Google uses Piper, a monorepo system (along with Gerrit for Git-based code reviews). Microsoft has Virtual File System for Git, formerly GVFS, to help overcome some of the scaling issues with Git. Meta has Sapling. But as the AI biz notes, Claude's code writing ability both created the situation and offered a way out through the creation of scalable code infrastructure tools – in addition to Scion, Claude helped conjure Antique (a code review interface), a code search tool, and a source control IAM system. The decentralized approach embodied by Git is the right one for most code repos, according to Anthropic. But the company's main branch weighs in at about 100 GB, with a compressed working copy at more than a quarter of that. "We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs," Anthropic said. "Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day." Even with the tools Git provides for working with portions of a codebase, Anthropic says operations proved challenging. Scion has been designed to meet the needs of AI agents, so the client leaves much of the work to the server; the source control queries are exposed via API so internal tools can respond without needing a local repo, and there's less synchronization but more need for server speed. "In Scion, the unit of work is a 'changeset,' an entry in a write-ahead log," Anthropic explains. "A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage." Work on Scion started in January, and when Claude Mythos Preview became available internally, Anthropic's code coaxers told the model to rewrite an early Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline. The much-hyped model produced a version that used 20 times less memory and ran four times as fast. When cost is no object thanks to ample venture funding, that sort of token spending just makes sense. Anthropic's Claude jockeys appear to be taking their obsolescence in stride. According to the AI biz, company developers who worked on Scion agree that Claude writes better code than they do. But they still possess a higher-level understanding that gives them a role as naysayers. "Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude 'no,'" Anthropic said. "Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place." "Just say no." As a slogan, it's timeless. And it's never been more relevant. Anthropic says its bespoke system isn't right for general use. There will be no open source release. Nonetheless, the company contends that its own code scaling problems will become commonplace in other organizations over the next few months, so it wanted to share its approach – having ample funding to pay for writing custom infrastructure tools. ®

articles.title: ESA targets Anbernic emulation handhelds as "superfake" piracy enablers
articles.text:
For years, Chinese hardware manufacturers have carved out a market niche with an array of handheld Android gaming devices focused on retro emulation and/or more modern game-streaming capabilities. Now, though, a major game industry trade group is targeting one of those manufacturers, Anbernic, asking the US Trade Representative (USTR) to add the company to its list of "Notorious Markets" that "engage in or facilitate substantial copyright piracy or trademark counterfeiting."

TorrentFreak was among the first to notice the request from the Entertainment Software Association (ESA), which was submitted to the USTR last week. In it, the US trade group—which represents major publishers including Nintendo, Microsoft, PlayStation, Amazon, Epic, EA, Ubisoft, and more—notes that Anbernic devices "are routinely offered or shipped with removable memory cards preloaded with hundreds or thousands of unauthorized copies of copyright-protected video games published by ESA members."

While many online sellers do include an SD card full of ROMs alongside emulation hardware of all types, Anbernic itself does not appear to do the same when selling directly from its website. Regardless, the ESA argues that these ROM-laden Anbernic devices selling through "normal retail channels" help to "normalize hardware-based piracy by delivering illicit catalogues through a polished consumer product." This, the ESA says, meets the threshold for a "superfake," an ill-defined designation that applies to "high-quality counterfeit trademark goods ... on a commercial scale."

articles.title: Topgolf saved over $11.3 million after leaving VMware
articles.text:
Topgolf’s VMware costs were going to increase by 400 percent under Broadcom. To avoid that cost, the sports entertainment company moved 12,000 virtual machines (VMs) to VergeIO’s VergeOS and has saved over $11 million so far.

Before migrating, Topgolf’s VMware connection “ran very deep,” Scott Forehand, Topgolf’s global infrastructure manager, told Ars Technica.

Topgolf has over 100 locations worldwide featuring interactive golf games with real-time shot tracking and digital analytics. The company used vSphere and ESXi for decades and started using VxRail, the hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) platform that VMware co-engineered with Dell, in 2017. articles.title: CISA director touts private partnerships after agency killed many
articles.text: The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has killed many of the industry partnerships it used to enhance security, but don't tell the organization's acting director. Speaking on Tuesday at a virtual public sector cyber resilience summit hosted by infosec firm Rubrik, Nick Andersen claimed that CISA’s public-private partnerships are the most critical aspect of his agency’s mission. “We don’t see everything. We’re not a law enforcement agency, intelligence agency, or a regulator,” Andersen said during a discussion at the summit. CISA, he added, relies on intelligence and insight not only from other government agencies and international partners, but from the private sector as well. CISA’s mission simply can’t succeed without motivating those various partners to share what they’ve seen, heard, and dealt with in order to build a comprehensive threat model. “It’s all carrots and partnerships,” Andersen added, referring to motivating partners to get on board with programs like CISA’s CI Fortify initiative for building resilient critical infrastructure. Were that actually the case, we wouldn’t really have a story to write here, but anyone who’s been following CISA’s trials and tribulations during the second Trump administration is likely to have raised an eyebrow at Andersen’s claims. Trump returned to office riding a wave of plans to cut government spending, which included massive reductions at CISA. Among the first CISA programs axed was the Cyber Safety Review Board, a public-private body set up by the Biden administration. In addition to that closure, the Trump administration also shuttered the Artificial Intelligence Safety and Security Board, Critical Infrastructure Partnership Advisory Council, National Security Telecommunications Advisory Committee, and US Secret Service Cyber Investigations Advisory Board, all bodies consisting of government and private players working together toward cybersecurity goals. Some of those bodies have since been stood up again or reformed under new names, wasting time and money that could have been better spent by cyber defenders doing things like, you know, advising CISA and other government agencies on security matters. CISA also terminated funding for and ties to the Center for Internet Security in late 2025. One of CISA’s bodies affected by the cut was the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a public-private partnership that shares threat intelligence and filters essential alerts down to the local government level. CISA staff has also been slashed considerably, with around a third of the Agency’s headcount, about 1,000 people, departing since Trump returned to office. CISA has since committed to rehiring around 300, but the Trump administration’s most recent budget request proposes eliminating an additional 900 positions at the agency, along with slashing nearly a billion dollars from CISA’s 2027 budget. When we asked about the apparent contradiction, CISA reached out to point us to initiatives like its reformed councils, CI Fortify, and security exercises it hosted with industry partners to test cyber resilience to point to the continued priority the agency places on its public-private partnerships. “CISA works with critical infrastructure owners and operators to assist them in securing both the physical security and cybersecurity of the systems and assets that support essential services,” an agency spokesperson told us. “Our regional teams assist industry and government partners across the country by assessing risks, helping entities bolster defenses and improve resilience, and responding promptly to threats.” But with so many outreach employees and general staff still missing, Andersen’s claims ring a bit hollow. Either the acting administrator is misrepresenting the continued importance of private industry partnerships at CISA, or he’s in denial about the state of his agency. Neither is great, especially with more budget and staffing cuts looming, and the price will be unprepared critical infrastructure. ®

articles.title: OpenAI's dot assistant burned 300K+ tokens in a day without a single prompt
articles.text: If you use OpenAI's dot, don't be surprised if it consumes a lot of tokens on its own. According to AI agent security and governance outfit Geordie, one dot agent produced 155 separate activity sequences and consumed more than 300,000 tokens - all without further human interaction, and all in the course of a day. Geordie has been testing the “always on” agentic assistant, dot, since OpenAI announced it in September, following in the footsteps of Meta Muse and Grok Bot. Compared to other personal agents, however, OpenAI’s dot “looked a little bit different,” Hanah-Marie Darley, Geordie chief AI officer, told The Register. “One of the things that we discovered really quickly was that they were really, really active without much user interaction.” For its testing, Darley gave dot read-only permissions, and she didn’t connect it to her personal apps, email, or other communications apps like Slack. The bot quickly went into research mode, collecting as much information as possible and surveying systems. “You can think about it very much like a new project manager coming in and taking a look at what's there, looking around to see what accesses you've given it, what accesses you have, and also what kind of systems you're running,” Darley said. The agent collects all of these data points into something akin to a daily journal entry, and continually updates those throughout the day. “If you've given it any tasks, it will effectively check on its own tasks, too,” Darley said. “But what was really unique was that the dot was spinning up agents without interacting with the user at all. It was all driven by the dot rather than a persistent or scheduled task from the user, or any user prompting.” 'Hyper-personalized,' and 'always-on' … what could possibly go wrong? Most enterprise AI agent usage tends to be custom-built bots, tasked with specific business projects, or agent harnesses like Claude, Codex, or Hero for AI-assisted engineering and coding, Darley said. “Those tend to be really driven by employees who are setting goals,” she told us during an interview. “But interestingly, personal agents set a lot more of their own tasks - and I don't think many people realize that as they start to play with them.” This is the whole value proposition of personal agents. Rather than passively waiting for user prompts, bots like Muse and dot aim to be proactive digital workers that perform multi-step tasks and connect to multiple apps, services, and accounts on the users’ behalf. “They’re trying to go hyper-personalized and collect as much context and information about you as possible to recommend things to you, and to be proactive,” Darley said. “But what that means is that they're effectively always on, operating in the background, and they have these active periods,” she added. Dot, in particular, is more proactive than other personal agents like Muse or Grok Bot, according to Darley. This doesn’t necessarily translate into higher token usage, she added. “They just operate differently.” For example, dots always operate with at least two agents running: The primary agent interacts with the user, and the secondary agent continuously runs in the background, collecting data. Dots and other agents can also spin up subagents for specific tasks. 50 traces in 2 minutes Of the dot-in-testing’s 155 agent traces, at least 50 of those happened within a two-minute period, and the majority occurred within a couple of hours, according to Darley. “Within one of the traces that we analyzed, the agent spun up multiple sub-agents that were short-lived, they would just do specific tasks, and fed the information from the existing accesses that had already been granted to the dot - and none of this was interacting with the user,” Darley said. Part of the evaluation involved testing a development system, and one of the dots spun up a sub-agent that checked all of the code repositories in the system. Meanwhile, another sub-agent continuously inventoried and tallied up all the data that it found while operating. “The user would have no idea that there were sub-agents working on their behalf,” she added. “They would have no idea how those agents were given access, or what their tasks were, which is really, really different from how most agents have been operating in business contexts.” The 155 traces cost Geordie about 307,000 tokens. Other requests cost anywhere from a couple hundred tokens to several thousand, depending on how much research the dot performs. “That’s really interesting because it's self-directed research,” Darley said. The user isn’t asking it to perform these tasks - or use a set number of tokens - but rather the dot does it on its own. Tokenomics Token costs vary widely depending on the user's location, subscription tier, discounted pricing arrangements, computing costs, and other terms and conditions. But for the purposes of our discussion, roughly 200,000 tokens consumed by a dot based on OpenAI’s Astra model cost between $5 and $10. “So if you think about what that’s going to look like every day, that could mean spending what you pay for a latte, depending on the city - but without any interaction with the user,” Darley said. “One of the things that a lot of people struggle with, especially when it comes to understanding their AI spend, is: How does token usage connect out to work product, or how does it connect out to results? And it's a hard one because it's not necessarily one to one,” she noted. One request to an LLM could cost 500 tokens and still be more valuable, from a business perspective, than another single request that cost 800,000 tokens. “It's really about how much compute does it cost you to get to a good answer, and that becomes a really subjective judgment,” Darley said. When it comes to dot and other always-on agents, however, she suspects “a lot of people aren’t going to be prepared for the background spend.” Do you know what your agents are doing? Just like employees did with chatbots, and then with coding agents, and now with personal agents: assume that people will bring dot and friends from home into their work life, Darley said. “Businesses are surprised often by the number of agents that are actively in their systems, even if they have a smaller rollout or a more controlled rollout in mind,” she said. “The second thing is not all agents act the same,” she added. “They operate with varying degrees of autonomy, with varying degrees of user input, and they're also really context driven. The best agents are the ones with the narrowest context because that means that they can pursue their goal with the right information at the right time.” Darley suggests organizations try the technology. She’s a self-described “massive AI optimist,” and says she believes agents can improve productivity and transform the way people work. AI isn’t going away, and, as such, businesses should familiarize themselves with agents. But she has one final warning before letting agents loose. “Don’t give them any personal information that you wouldn't be comfortable sending in an email,” Darley said. “And don’t put real money on it - like your personal cards. Buy it a Visa gift card, if you want to give it access to make purchases for you. Oftentimes, people don’t think about that until something goes wrong.” ®

articles.title: Flights to Saudi Arabia suspended until Oct 17
articles.text: Mumbai: Airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia until October 17 after the kingdom's aviation regulator suspended operations at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, disrupting travel across the region and leaving passengers seeking alternative routes.Air India, Air India Express and IndiGo have suspended services to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah, with IndiGo also suspending flights to Medina, according to an advisory issued by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh on Tuesday. Akasa Air has also suspended flights to Riyadh and Jeddah until the same date.The disruption has spread to international carriers. Emirates cancelled multiple services to Riyadh, Dammam, Jeddah and Medina on October 12 and 13, while Etihad Airways cancelled Abu Dhabi-Riyadh flights through October 19 and services to Jeddah and Dammam through October 14. Flydubai has reported cancellations affecting Riyadh, Dammam and Abha through October 19. Qatar Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam without announcing a resumption date. Gulf Air has cancelled Riyadh services through October 17.European carriers have also extended disruptions. Lufthansa Group has cancelled Riyadh flights through October 16, while Air France-KLM has suspended services to the Saudi capital through the end of October. Philippine Airlines has extended its Riyadh suspension until November 29.The suspensions come after an attack at Riyadh airport on October 10 killed Indian national Mohammed Yousef Ali and injured 11 others. Four of the injured Indians remain in intensive care, four are receiving treatment in hospital wards and three have been discharged, the embassy said.While operations at Riyadh airport have been suspended, flights at other major Saudi airports, including Dammam, Jeddah and Medina, continue, though they face disruptions. Saudi carriers Saudia and Flynas are operating some scheduled services, according to the embassy.The disruption is forcing passengers to check alternative travel options as airlines adjust their schedules. Indian nationals needing to leave Saudi Arabia in an emergency can consider flights from neighbouring Gulf countries, particularly Qatar and Bahrain, subject to obtaining the required visas, the embassy said.It advised Indian nationals to remain in contact with their airlines to verify flight status. It also said Saudi authorities would allow visitors, tourists, Umrah pilgrims and business travellers who overstayed their visas because flights were unavailable to leave without paying fines.The Indian Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah continue to operate normally. The embassy has opened a 24-hour control room to assist Indian nationals as the situation evolves.

Apple unleashes a swarm of Mac Minions to share GPU resources for large AI tasks
articles.text: In an effort to give its employees better access to GPU resources for inference tasks, Apple has rounded up its Minions, not the animated yellow creatures, but a distributed system that puts idle GPUs across its Macs to work on AI workloads. Apple researchers describe it as "a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads." Apple's researchers said the company has used Minions to make GPU compute more readily available to its teams. "Prior to its adoption, some inference jobs experienced queue times exceeding ten hours due to limited centralized GPU availability," the paper on Minions explains. "With Minions, tasks can often begin execution within minutes by leveraging idle macOS devices." Apple's recently released Mac mini and Mac Studio support clustering using RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) over Thunderbolt 5, allowing compute and memory to be combined to support a single AI workload. This allows, for example, loading a model too large for a single machine to accommodate. Minions is designed to create a virtual GPU cloud from connected Mac hardware to create a fault-tolerant pool of inference workers in a shared distributed inference platform. So instead of sitting idle, GPU resources can be used more readily by teams on the network. It's not necessarily intended as a way to run large models as much as it is to redistribute idle resources on the network. Minions has four primary components: Minion Server, PostgreSQL Metadata Store, Minion Executor, and Minion Watchdog. The Minion Server provides the coordination layer, receiving user requests and making them available as subtasks. The Minion Executor runs inference tasks on a Mac's GPU, uploads the results to S3, and reports execution status through the Minion Server, which maintains task metadata in PostgreSQL. And the Minion Watchdog monitors this process for failures – like one of the Macs in the network not responding – and re-assigns tasks if needed. Database stats get fed to Grafana-based dashboards for real-time visibility. Apple's approach, which focuses on hardware availability and utilization, is not the same as an Nvidia cluster, which focuses on throughput, latency, and efficient GPU utilization for large models. ®

articles.title: Claude submitted fake murder tip to Philly police during summertime testing
articles.text: An Anthropic AI model submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide through an online form run by the Philadelphia Police Department (PPD). The tip, filed July 18 through PhillyUnsolvedMurders[.]com by “someone who might have information about the case,” went straight into the inbox’s spam folder. Anthropic discovered it on September 28, notified the PPD on October 7, and sent representatives to the police HQ the following day. Anthropic told the police the AI submitted the tip during a test exercise that involved interacting with randomly selected websites. The PPD said its findings are so far consistent with Anthropic's account. Because the tip was flagged as spam, it never reached the department's Real-Time Crime Center. The PPD said officers vet all submissions, automated or otherwise, before forwarding them to investigators, and that this process safeguards against abuse of the tip system. It added that this does not “diminish the seriousness” of an AI submitting fabricated information. “The city of Philadelphia takes this incident very seriously,” the PPD said. “The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable.” It added: “The department and the [Cherelle] Parker administration will continue to closely monitor this incident, and will provide more information to the public as soon as it becomes available. In addition to our investigation into this incident, the Parker administration will explore all necessary regulatory protections going forward locally along with our state and federal partners.” On October 9, Anthropic published a report on this and other AI errors. The report covered four categories of AI failures, including vulnerability exploits, access to restricted data, bypassing fetch tool limits with URL shorteners, and submitting false information via web forms. Anthropic declined to name any of the affected organizations, other than the PPD after the department went public. Some cases involved local, state, and federal US government websites, though the AI company didn't say which of the four categories they fell under. The PPD did not name the model responsible, but Anthropic said Claude Haiku 4.5 was tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected web pages, and hinted at the model not being prompted specifically enough. “Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions,” Anthropic's report stated. The fake tip read: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Anthropic said the incident was less severe than the cyberattacks over the summer. The report said: “Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.” By contrast, the "dishonesty" displayed over the summer was “sustained over hours” and supported continued attacks, the Claude maker said. Anthropic said it will keep reporting these failures when it detects them, and will continue fine-tuning behavioral and alignment training. The 3,095-word report contained no apology.®

Anthropic conjures another threat that doesn't exist yet to stoke fears of AI apocalypse
articles.text: Nothing sells AI products as well as fear. Using new research, Anthropic claims that self-replicating AI worms could be just months away from spreading across vulnerable IoT devices, which would be a problem if it came true. The frontier lab published a research report Monday suggesting that AI models could eventually self-replicate without relying on datacenter hardware, with a 9-billion-parameter model successfully setting up inference on eight of the nine hardware types Anthropic tested. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off,” Anthropic warned, adding that such an AI worm could also suss out the workings of unfamiliar devices, potentially making it more adaptable than conventional botnets like Mirai, Kimwolf (the representative IoT botnet threat model used in the study), and others. Anthropic’s researchers managed to get a distributed instance of Gemma4-26B-A4B running across 15 generic Android set-top streaming boxes - a common target of traditional botnet malware due to their lax security. Once up and running, the distributed Gemma4 model was able to conduct inference tasks at a blistering 0.39 tokens per second. That, says Anthropic, proves that AI models can conduct inference with their various layers distributed across cheap hardware, but it doesn't prove such a model could self-replicate. For that, the researchers turned to Z.ai’s GLM 5.2. GLM was used to propagate a copy of Llama3.1-8B across eight Google Cloud instances running an Android 15 emulator in a virtual private cloud, which Anthropic said it was able to do with a high degree of success, with the model successfully spreading to all eight nodes in four out of five trials, and seven of eight in the other. “It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process,” Anthropic explained. Sanity check: This isn’t going to end the world, either Frontier AI labs have become adept at publishing findings that portend doom that only they can prevent. Doing more than a cursory reading of this report suggests that this threat is just as deserving of a big, honking asterisk as the rest. Take, for example, what is needed for an AI model to exploit vulnerabilities and spread to various systems. One would think that such an element would be an important part of demonstrating the danger of a self-replicating AI botnet, but Anthropic decided it didn’t need to worry about that for this study. “We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process, since earlier papers CyberGym, ExploitBench, and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools,” Anthropic explained in the writeup. In other words, the replication these models managed to achieve was done on nodes that were custom-built for this project and deliberately left open to attack, although the draggingly slow inference demonstration ran on real, inexpensive Android TV boxes. As Anthropic notes, AI models can also benefit from being given the right tools to turn them into capable cyberattack agents. There was a custom-built harness called Memento involved in this scenario too. Are IoT nodes that get hijacked by botnets famously insecure? Yes, but it doesn’t take much to prevent the most common ingress routes – that’s just good security hygiene that has nothing to do with the involvement of AI. Anthropic acknowledged that its deliberately simplified exploitation tests provided “an upper bound on real-world success.” Then there’s the aforementioned speed. Anthropic says such AI worms would be challenging to shut down, but estimates that they might take days to double in size. When Mirai appeared on the scene in 2016, it was doubling in around an hour. Anthropic points out that speed is a factor in detection and mitigation, too. AI models are not simple malware packages: They’re massive things that would eat up tons of bandwidth and quickly point to their sources. As an AI botnet grew, that traffic could become more noticeable, making infected devices easier to detect. Finally, end-to-end replication may have been successful with GLM-5.2, but that’s it. Anthropic tested other open-weight models, and they all “fail[ed] reliably,” according to the report. Anthropic didn’t mention how many models it tested. The report also mentions that GLM’s unique success has another important condition: It assumes its capabilities “could be packed into Llama3.1-8B,” stacking another assumption onto this latest house of doomsaying AI cards. “Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end,” Anthropic said, while noting that GLM-5.2 was capable of end-to-end replication, conveniently leaving out all the important caveats. Anthropic further admits that it has no idea "exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take,” or when it might arise, if ever. “If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year,” the company added – again imposing an essential condition on this supposed threat. “As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” the company said at the end of its report. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.” Here to stay for a given value of not existing yet, of course. Yet again, a frontier lab is warning us of a threat that doesn’t exist yet – at least in this case, basic security measures could make life harder for any future AI-powered botnet. ®
